pr.title: Do not trim paths in MIR validator
pr.author: compiler-errors

processing.reason: This PR's historical wrong state is compiler-internal and not a source-level value transformation: `validate_types` ran the type checker without `with_no_trimmed_paths`, so validation/inlining could format type names with path trimming or trigger a compiler diagnostic/ICE. The supplied regression is explicitly `//@ build-pass` with `-Zinline-mir` and has no runtime value output to compare. Modeling this as ordinary Rust functions would require inventing a local path-trimming mechanism and manufacturing differing numeric/boolean/character return values, which is not the actual historical transformation and would violate the requirement not to force an unrelated difference. Therefore no source-grounded original/transformed pair can be validated with Miri here.

analysis.summary: The MIR Validator's type checker formatted type names (including with `{ty:?}` Debug) while running without disabling diagnostic path trimming. Because the inliner also invokes the Validator, and inlining can produce validation failures even for valid code (notably around where clauses and rigid projections), the Validator could encounter type-formatting/path-trimming behavior outside the normal error path. The fix wraps the whole `visit_body` call in `with_no_trimmed_paths!` and switches many type-name format arguments from Debug (`{:?}`/`{:#?}`) to Display (`{}`), and adds a build-pass regression test using `-Zinline-mir`.
analysis.originalLogic: `validate_types` created a `TypeChecker` and executed `type_checker.visit_body(body);` directly, with no suppression of diagnostic path trimming. Validation failure paths constructed messages with `format!` using type Debug formatting such as `format!("bad index ({index_ty:?} != usize)")`, `format!("{base_ty:?} dereferenced after ElaborateBoxDerefs")`, and `format!("Failed subtyping {ty:#?} and {:#?}", ...)`. The inliner also uses this validator, so these type-name strings can be formatted during inlining rather than only on an ordinary diagnostic error path.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: Historically, the Validator ran the type-checker visitor without `with_no_trimmed_paths`, and formatted MIR types with Debug (`{ty:?}` / `{ty:#?}`), allowing path trimming to be engaged during validation/type formatting in the inliner context. The corrected implementation instead wraps the visitor in `with_no_trimmed_paths!({ type_checker.visit_body(body); })` and uses Display (`{ty}`) for type-name fields. The essential corrected invariant is that validator type formatting must not depend on diagnostic path trimming; the Debug-to-Display changes accompany that invariant but should not be treated as the sole semantic fix.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust programs compiled with MIR inlining enabled (`-Zinline-mir`), especially code whose inlining causes validation failures even though the source is valid: traits with associated types and `?Sized` buffers, const-generic array types, unsizing/coercion between `Wrap<Array<N>>` and `Wrap<Slice>`, and functions carrying where clauses that mention the trait/associated-type projections. The supplied regression test is `tests/ui/mir/inline-causes-trimmed-paths.rs` with `//@ build-pass` and `//@ compile-flags: -Zinline-mir`.
analysis.trigger: MIR inlining invokes the Validator and validation emits a failure message that formats a type name, while the type formatter is allowed to trim paths even though this is not the ordinary diagnostic error path. In the regression test, `coerce` calls `coerce_again`, returning `&Wrap<Slice>` from `&Wrap<Array<N>>`, with `Wrap<S: Storage> { _b: S::Buffer }`; `main` constructs `Wrap<Array<1>>` and coerces it to `&Wrap<Slice>`.
preconditions: The MIR Validator's type checker is invoked during inlining, not only during ordinary diagnostic reporting.
Validation constructs type-name strings with type formatting (historically Debug formatting).

The program involves trait associated types / rigid projections and where clauses; the regression test uses `trait Storage { type Buffer: ?Sized; }`, `Wrap<S: Storage>`, and a `where Array<N>: Storage` clause.
The source can be valid Rust even when an inlining-induced validation failure occurs; the regression test is expected to build successfully.
pitfalls: Do not reduce the fix to merely changing `{:?}` to `{}`: the key invariant is disabling path trimming around the whole validator visitor with `with_no_trimmed_paths!`.
Do not assume every validation failure implies invalid source: the patch states that inlining can cause validation errors even for valid code, mostly around where clauses and rigid projections.
Do not require an expected stderr/error output for this regression: the new test is `//@ build-pass`.
Do not wrap only individual formatting calls; the patch wraps `type_checker.visit_body(body);` so all type formatting during validation runs without trimmed paths.
Formatting type names can have behavior beyond producing a message, so invoking it eagerly in validation is not semantically neutral.
analysis.testStrategy: Add and run a UI build-pass test with MIR inlining: `tests/ui/mir/inline-causes-trimmed-paths.rs` marked `//@ build-pass` and `//@ compile-flags: -Zinline-mir`. Define `trait Storage { type Buffer: ?Sized; }`; implement it for `Array<const N: usize>` with `type Buffer = [(); N];` and for `Slice` with `type Buffer = [()];`; define `struct Wrap<S: Storage> { _b: S::Buffer }`; define `fn coerce<const N: usize>(this: &Wrap<Array<N>>) -> &Wrap<Slice> where Array<N>: Storage { coerce_again(this) }` and `fn coerce_again<const N: usize>(this: &Wrap<Array<N>>) -> &Wrap<Slice> { this }`; in `main`, build `let inner: Wrap<Array<1>> = Wrap { _b: [(); 1] };` and assert the coercion with `let _: &Wrap<Slice> = coerce(&inner);`. Compile this program; success is the regression signal. To construct a differing-input pair for study, keep the source identical and compare compilations where the validator runs without `with_no_trimmed_paths` versus with it; do not claim observed execution or reproduction from this historical patch.
evidence: Do not trim paths in MIR validator
